title: Malware, web attacks, cloud & IoT
syllabusUnit: Unit V: Software Vulnerabilities, Web Exploits & Emerging Threats
covers: Viruses/worms/ransomware, DoS/DDoS, SQL injection, XSS, cloud and IoT security basics
learningGoals: You will be able to distinguish viruses, worms, and ransomware.
You will be able to demonstrate how parameterized queries prevent SQL Injection (SQLi).
You will be able to explain Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and IoT security constraints.

lessonCards.title: The Malware Zoo: Viruses vs Worms
lessonCards.analogy: A virus needs a host file to hitchhike; a worm is an autonomous creature that crawls across network cables on its own.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Viruses attach to legitimate executable files. Worms self-replicate and spread across network vulnerabilities without user interaction. Ransomware encrypts files and demands cryptocurrency extortion.
lessonCards.example: WannaCry in 2017 was a worm-ransomware hybrid that infected 200,000 systems in hours using EternalBlue.

lessonCards.title: SQL Injection: Break the Query
lessonCards.analogy: Tricking a bank teller by writing 'Give me Alice's balance OR 1=1 (which is always true!)' on the deposit slip.
lessonCards.coreConcept: SQL Injection occurs when untrusted user input is directly concatenated into database queries: ' OR '1'='1 -- bypasses authentication entirely.
lessonCards.example: Defense: Always use Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements) so input is treated as literal data, never executable code.

lessonCards.title: XSS & The Internet of Fragile Things
lessonCards.analogy: Sneaking a malicious JavaScript post-it note into a shared bulletin board that executes in every visitor's browser.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Stored and Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) injects malicious scripts into web apps to steal session cookies. IoT devices (cameras, smart plugs) have weak CPUs, hardcoded default passwords, and no automatic updates.
lessonCards.example: The Mirai botnet enslaved 300,000 IoT devices with default logins to launch historic 1 Tbps DDoS floods.

questions.prompt: What is the single most effective defense against SQL Injection (SQLi) vulnerabilities in web applications?
options: Using Parameterized Queries (Prepared Statements)
Using complex CSS styles
Shortening user passwords to 4 characters
Running database servers on port 80
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries pre-compile SQL commands, ensuring user input is strictly treated as variable values, completely preventing input from altering SQL logic.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Prepared statements make SQL injection mathematically impossible in application code.
CSS only changes visual styling.
Short passwords drastically weaken authentication.
Databases should never be exposed to public web ports.
questions.realWorldExample: OWASP lists injection flaws as a top perennial threat in the OWASP Top 10 web security risks.

questions.prompt: How does a computer 'Worm' differ from a classic computer 'Virus'?
options: A worm is self-replicating and spreads autonomously across networks without requiring user execution of a host file
A worm only attacks wooden computers
A virus only runs on Android
A worm requires clicking a link
questions.explanation: Viruses require a human to run an infected file. Worms scan networks, exploit unpatched vulnerabilities, and copy themselves without any human intervention.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Autonomous network propagation defines a worm.
Physical humor.
Viruses infect all operating systems.
Clicking links describes trojan or phishing delivery.
questions.realWorldExample: The 1988 Morris Worm was the first internet worm; it accidentally brought down 10% of the ARPANET.

questions.prompt: In Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), what is the attacker's primary objective inside the victim's web browser?
options: To execute unauthorized JavaScript in the victim's session (e.g. stealing session cookies or authentication tokens)
To format the victim's hard drive
To download more RAM
To change the computer's wallpaper
questions.explanation: XSS allows attackers to execute client-side scripts in the security context of the victim's browser session, accessing document.cookie and impersonating the user.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Executing rogue JavaScript to hijack sessions is the core goal of XSS.
Browsers run in sandboxes and cannot format hard drives directly.
RAM is physical hardware.
Wallpapers are local OS settings.
questions.realWorldExample: Content Security Policy (CSP) headers and context-aware output encoding neutralize XSS attacks.

questions.prompt: What technique is used in a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) 'Amplification Attack' (e.g. NTP or DNS amplification)?
options: Sending small requests with spoofed victim source IPs to public servers that reply with massive data streams to the victim
Sending encrypted emails to friends
Overclocking computer monitors
Running antivirus scans repeatedly
questions.explanation: Attackers forge the victim's return IP address in small UDP requests; intermediate servers send huge multi-kilobyte responses flooding the victim's bandwidth.
wrongExplanations: Correct! UDP spoofing + high response-to-request size multiplier creates massive amplification floods.
Email is unrelated.
Monitors do not generate network bandwidth.
Antivirus runs locally.
questions.realWorldExample: Memcached UDP amplification attacks achieved historic traffic reflection ratios of over 50,000 to 1.

questions.prompt: Why are consumer Internet of Things (IoT) devices frequently hijacked into massive botnets?
options: They often ship with hardcoded default credentials, lack automatic firmware patches, and run minimal unmonitored Linux builds
Because IoT devices are too expensive
Because smart lightbulbs have supercomputers inside
Because IoT devices use quantum encryption
questions.explanation: Consumers rarely update or change default factory passwords on smart cameras and routers, leaving them permanently exposed to automated scanning scripts.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Weak security defaults and lack of patching make IoT devices prime targets for botnet recruitment.
Cost does not prevent patching.
IoT devices use cheap low-power microcontrollers.
IoT devices rarely feature post-quantum crypto.
questions.realWorldExample: The Mirai botnet scanned the internet for busybox devices with default logins 'admin:admin' to build a 600 Gbps DDoS weapon.

questions.prompt: How does modern 'Ransomware' extort victim organizations?
options: It encrypts victim databases with strong symmetric ciphers and demands cryptocurrency payment in exchange for the private decryption key
It deletes all emails from last year
It changes all file names to upper-case
It plays loud music through computer speakers
questions.explanation: Ransomware generates local symmetric keys to encrypt enterprise file servers, encrypts those keys with the attacker's public RSA key, and demands ransom.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Strong encryption locks access to operational data until ransom is paid.
Ransomware holds active files hostage, not just old archives.
Case renaming is cosmetic.
Audio tricks are harmless pranks.
questions.realWorldExample: The Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack in 2021 halted fuel delivery across the US East Coast for days.

ashRecap: Never concatenate user input directly into SQL queries—always use Parameterized Statements! Keep your IoT devices patched and change default passwords immediately!
